Acid, Base and Salt

Acid

  • An acid is any hydrogen-containing substance that is capable of donating a proton (hydrogen ion → H⁺) to another substance.
  • Acids are usually identified by their sour taste.
  • An acid turns blue litmus paper red.

Base

  • A base is a molecule or ion able to accept a hydrogen ion from an acid.
  • A base turns red litmus paper blue.
  • Litmus is a purple dye, which changes its colour when interacted with acid or base.

Acid-Base Indicators

  1. 1. Natural Indicators: Natural indicators are substances, often derived from plants, that change color in the presence of acids or bases, indicating their acidic or basic nature.
  • E.g.
  1. 1. Litmus: It is extracted from Lichen (Thallophyte).
  2. 2. Turmeric: It is a natural dye Circumin is present in it.
  3. 3. Coloured petals: Coloured petals of Hydrangea, Petunia, Geranium, Red Cabbage, China Rose, etc.
  4. 2. Synthetic Indicator: Synthetic indicators are acid-base indicators that are man-made or synthesized in a laboratory.
  • E.g.
  1. 1. Phenolphthalein: It is colourless in acidic solutions but turns pink in basic solutions.
  2. 2. Methyl Orange: It is red in acidic solutions and yellow in basic solutions.
IndicatorAcidBase
LitmusBlue to RedRed to Blue
TurmericRemains yellowTurn to reddish brown
PhenolphthaleinColourlessPink
Methyl orangeRedYellow (a bit orangey)

Olfactory Indicators

  • An olfactory indicator is a substance whose smell changes based on whether it is mixed with an acid or base. E.g. Vanilla, Onion, Clove, etc.

Universal Indicators

  • A universal indicator is a mixture of different types of indicators that exhibits different coloration at different levels.
  • It is used to detect the acidic or basic nature of a substance or a solution.

Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases

  1. 1. Reaction with Metals
  • When acids react with metals, they typically produce a salt and hydrogen gas, while some metals like zinc and aluminium also react with bases to form a salt and hydrogen gas.
  • Acid + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen gas (Burns with a pop sound)
  • Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂ (g)
  • Zn + NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂ (g)
  • Sodium Hydroxide: Strong base
  • Magnesium Hydroxide: Mild base
  1. 2. Reaction of Metal Carbonate and Metal Hydrogen Carbonate with Acids
  • When acids react with metal carbonates or metal hydrogen carbonates, they produce a salt, carbon dioxide gas, and water.
  • Metal Carbonate OR Metal Bicarbonate + Acid → Salt + CO₂ + H₂O
  • Na₂CO₃/NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + CO₂ + H₂O

Test of Carbon Dioxide

  • Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) turns lime water milky because the carbon dioxide reacts with the calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂) in the lime water, forming an insoluble white precipitate of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).
  • Ca(OH)₂ (aq) + CO₂ (g) → CaCO₃ (s) + H₂O (l)
  • (Calcium Hydroxide / Carbon dioxide / Calcium carbonate / Water)
  • (lime water / (white ppt) / Turns lime water milky)

Acid/Base in Water Solution

Conduction of Electricity

  • Aqueous solutions of acids and bases conduct electricity because they contain charged particles (ions) that can move and carry an electric current, which is due to the dissociation of acids into H⁺ ions and bases into OH⁻ ions.
  • Distilled water, alcohol and glucose do not conduct electricity.
  • All bases do not dissolve in water. E.g. copper (II) oxide.
  • An alkali is a base that dissolve in water.
  • All alkali are bases, but all bases are not alkali.

Dilution of Acids

  • While diluting an acid, it's safer to add acid to water slowly and with constant stirring than to add water to an acid. Adding water to acid can cause an extreme exothermic reaction that produces a large amount of heat which can cause the solution to boil, splatter, and cause burns.

To Concentrated Acid → Diluted Acid

Neutralisation Reaction

  • A neutralization reaction is a type of acid-base reaction where an acid reacts with a base to form salt and water to release heat (exothermic reaction), essentially "cancelling out" each other's acidic or basic properties.
  • Acid + Base → Salt + Water + Heat
  • Metal oxide + Acid → Salt + H₂O (Basic)
  • Non-metal oxide + Base → Salt + H₂O (Acidic)

Strong Acid + Weak Base → Salt (Acidic) + H₂O

  • E.g. Al(OH)₃ + HCl → AlCl₃ (Acidic salt) + H₂O

Weak Acid + Strong Base → Salt (Basic) + H₂O

  • E.g. CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa (basic salt) + H₂O

Strong Acid + Strong Base → Salt (neutral) + H₂O

  • E.g. NaOH + HCl → NaCl (neutral salt) + H₂O

Weak Acid + Weak Base → Salt (neutral) + H₂O

  • E.g. CH₃COOH + NH₄OH → CH₃COONH₄ (neutral) + H₂O

pH Scale

  • "p" stands for "Potenz" means "Power" in German language.
  • pH scale was developed by Lauritz Sorensen (a Danish chemist).
  • It is an universal indicator (a mixture of several indicators) and a logarithmic scale.
  • It shows different colour at different hydrogen ion concentration.
  • It measures H⁺ ion concentration.
  • pH = -log [H⁺]

Importance of pH Scale in Everyday Life

  • Human body works is a narrow pH range of 7–7.8.
  • pH scale is used in treatment of soil (Quick lime/CaCO₃/Slaked lime is added to acidic soil).
  • When soil is too basic, then gypsum is added to treat it.

Important pH Values

  • Gastric juice: 1.6
  • Lemon: 2
  • Milk: 6.4
  • Blood: 7.4 (slightly alkaline)
  • Saliva: 6.5
  • Milk of Magnesia: 10
  • NaOH: 14
  • Antacids like Mg(OH)₂ → Milk of Magnesia, baking soda, aluminium hydroxide is used to treat indigestion when stomach produces too much HCl.
  • pH levels help in self-defence in plants and animals.
  1. 1. Bee sting: It contains methanoic acid/formic acid (causes burning sensation when it comes in contact with skin). Remedy: A mild base like Calamine lotion (contains Zinc carbonate) is applied.
  2. 2. Nettle plant leaves: Sting of the hair of the nettle leaves contain methanoic acid. Remedy: The juice of dock leaves is applied due to its basic properties which relieves the burning or stinging sensation.
  • Acid rain occurs when pH of the rainwater drops below 5.6 (contains sulphur dioxide (SO₂) + nitrogen oxides).
  • Tooth decay starts when the pH value is less than 5.5.

Chlor-Alkali Process

  • The chlor-alkali process is an industrial method that uses electrolysis to produce chlorine, hydrogen, and sodium hydroxide (caustic soda).
  • An aqueous solution of sodium chloride (NaCl) or brine is passed through an electrolytic cell. An electric current is passed through the solution. Chlorine gas (Chlor) and sodium hydroxide (Alkali) solution are produced.
  • 2NaCl (aq) + 2H₂O → 2NaOH (aq) + Cl₂ (g) + H₂ (g)
  • (At Cathode / At Anode / At Cathode)

Bleaching Powder

  • Its chemical formula is CaOCl₂ (calcium oxychloride/calcium hypochlorite).
  • It is commonly known as Chlorinated Lime.
  • It is produced by the action of chlorine on dry Slaked Lime (Ca(OH)₂).
  • Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O (Slaked Lime/Lime Water)

Uses of Bleaching Powder

  • It is used for bleaching cotton and linen clothes in textile industries.
  • It is used for bleaching wood pulp in paper industries.
  • It is used in laundry.
  • It is used as an oxidising agent in chemical industry.
  • It is used as an disinfectant for cleaning drinking water.

Baking Soda

  • Its chemical formula is NaHCO₃ (sodium bicarbonate).
  • Sodium chloride, water, carbon dioxide, and ammonia react to produce sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) and ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl).
  • NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ + NH₃ → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl
  • (Sublime compound)

When Baking Soda is Heated

  • When baking soda is heated, it undergoes a decomposition reaction, breaking down into sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃), water (H₂O), and carbon dioxide (CO₂).

Uses of Baking Soda

  • It is used to make tasty, crispy pakora and used in faster cooking.
  • It is used to make baking powder = mixture of baking soda + mild edible acid.
  • It is used as antacids (substances which neutralise stomach acidity).
  • It is used in soda-acid fire extinguisher (Dilute H₂SO₄ + NaHCO₃).

Soda-Acid Fire Extinguisher: When the fire extinguisher's knob is turned, the sulfuric acid and sodium bicarbonate react to produce carbon dioxide gas.

Washing Soda

  • Its chemical formula is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (hydrated sodium carbonate).
  • NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂
  • Na₂CO₃ + 10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·10H₂O

Uses of Washing Soda

  • It is used in glass, soap and paper industries.
  • It is used in manufacturing of borax (Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O).
  • It is used as a cleaning agent.
  • It is used in removing permanent hardness of water.
  • Hard water: It is a type of water that contains high levels of calcium and magnesium minerals.
  • Heavy water (D₂O): It is a type of water that contains a higher concentration of deuterium (a heavy isotope of hydrogen) than regular water.

Plaster of Paris

  • On heating Gypsum at 373 K, it loses water molecules and form Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O → Calcium Sulphate Hemihydrate).
  • It is a white powder and on mixing with water, it changes to Gypsum.
  • CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O
  • (Plaster of Paris) → (Gypsum)

Uses of Plaster of Paris

  • It is used to support fractured bones, forming a hard cast that immobilizes the injured limb while it heals.
  • It is used for making toys, decorative materials, smooth surface of walls, etc.

Note

It is always stored in moisture proof container, as it absorbs moisture to form hard Gypsum.

Some Other Salts

  • Blue vitriol: CuSO₄·5H₂O (it can be used to relieve mouth ulcers).
  • Green vitriol: FeSO₄·7H₂O
  • White vitriol: ZnSO₄·7H₂O
  • Mohr's Salt: (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O
  • Alum: KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O
  • Epsom salt: MgSO₄·7H₂O

Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white or pale green in colour and has a powdery appearance.
